description: We are a team of four Salvadorans united by curiosity, technology, and a desire to create solutions with real impact. We are participating in this challenge to represent El Salvador, combine our different skills, and show that great ideas can come from a small country. Our team brings together creativity, analysis, innovation, and collaboration to turn a challenge into a meaningful and practical solution.
summary:
IGNIS Orbit 503 is a geospatial intelligence platform that visualizes and analyzes fire activity data collected by the MODIS and VIIRS satellite sensors, focusing exclusively on El Salvador. Its main objective is to support data-driven decision-making based on historical information, enabling the identification of patterns and the analysis of fire activity trends across the country. The platform transforms complex satellite data into accessible and actionable insights through an interactive map, historical trend analysis, anomaly detection, and geographic and temporal filters. Additionally, it enables users to explore the spatial and temporal distribution of fire detections, providing a comprehensive understanding of fire activity patterns across different regions of El Salvador. It aims to support environmental monitoring, scientific research, and the development of fire prevention and risk management strategies by leveraging Earth observation data to inform decisions and strengthen national environmental analysis capabilities.

GitHub Organization: https://github.com/NASA-Space-Apps-Orbit-503

GitHub Organization: https://github.com/NASA-Space-Apps-Orbit-503

IGNIS Orbit 503 is a project that aims to present a solution to the challenge "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots" by providing a two-part answer to the problem.

First, a process of harmonization and coalescence of data from the MODIS and VIIRS sensors into a single, continuous dataset. This dataset can be used as a historical time-series source for analysis, exploration, and prediction. It is agnostic of the presentation layer and able to process data for any geographic zone provided.

Harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS aims to join the fire hotspot records from both sensors into a single time series, so that older MODIS data and current VIIRS data can be compared. This is necessary because VIIRS, with pixels of about 375 m compared with 1 km for MODIS, detects smaller fires, and both satellites also pass over at different times of day and use different algorithms and thresholds. To make them comparable, the data are usually resampled to a common grid, detections are matched in space and time, and fire radiative power is used as the reference metric.

Second, a client-facing webpage that allows users to visualize the processed data and eases access to it and its analysis through a clear, intuitive, and user-friendly interface. The interface is divided into three topics: Explore All Data, Historical Trends, and Anomalies. Each section consists of:

  • A series of filters that allow selecting date ranges, longitude and latitude, instruments, and satellites.
  • A map showing the data filtered according to the parameters set in the filters, with tooltips providing more information.
  • Tables detailing the requested data for Historical Trends and Anomalies.
  • Graphs showing historical trends, occurrences of anomalies, and related data.

What benefits does it have?

  • It allows the harmonization of, easy access to, and study of the data from both instruments. This helps the transition from MODIS, which is being decommissioned, to VIIRS. It does so through a single dataset and a reusable pipeline that permits creating continuous, compatible temporal data series. Users no longer need to reconcile different measures and parameters each time a new measurement or place is added or needed, and the result is agnostic to the tool consuming it.
  • It provides a user-facing webpage that allows quick retrieval of processed data and visualization to study historical trends, the already united data, and graphs and analysis of the information, without the need to create new maps.

What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Scientists, fire managers, and anyone interested in or using fire data provided by MODIS and VIIRS.
  • Researchers and analysts who monitor and plan around wildfires.
  • The creation of open, long-term fire records across different instruments without disruption.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Architecture: client-server, divided into a webpage created with Vue.js and a backend API service made with Rust, connected to a DuckDB database to handle the growing amount of data.
  • Deployment: Dokploy and GitHub Pages.
  • Maps: Leaflet and OpenStreetMap.
  • Hardware: four personal laptops.
  • Version control: Git.
  • Data source: NASA FIRMS.
  • Pipeline POC: Google Colab, Python

How is your project creative?

  • Beyond harmonizing the data, we make it usable by people who are not remote-sensing specialists. A simple dashboard/interface lets users explore hot spots by region and date without GIS software, and the pipeline output is designed for low-connectivity use, e.g., downloadable summaries or lightweight files.
  • Focusing on El Salvador turns the dataset into a decision tool. During the dry season, the harmonized hot spots can help the Ministry of Environment distinguish likely agricultural burns from wildfires, and help farmers/local cooperatives see where and when burning happens near their land.

What factors did your team consider?

The factors considered were the time constraint of two days, the large amount of data from 20 years of recording by sensors and satellites in many locations, and the limited resources available to a group of four people.

Because of the time constraints, and to provide a deliverable that is as complete as possible, the data and maps have been limited to El Salvador, our team’s country of residence. However, the project is scalable and adjustable to other countries or whole regions of the world with little modification to the original code.
